summary: Describes a way for BGP/MPLS VPN providers to reduce how many provider edge routers must hold all routes of a VPN, by letting only a subset do so. Under some conditions it can also reduce bandwidth waste when multicast traffic uses ingress replication.

eli5.summary: Not every mailroom needs a copy of the whole city map. Only a few keep it, and the rest ask them, saving space.

subtitle: How a BGP/MPLS VPN provider can keep a full copy of a VPN's routes on only a few routers.

tldr.problem: In an any-to-any BGP/MPLS VPN, every Provider Edge (PE) router attached to a VPN site has to hold all of that VPN's routes.
tldr.mechanism: Some PEs become Virtual Hubs and keep every route. The rest become Virtual Spokes, which keep only their own sites' routes plus a VPN-IP default route from their hub. Route Targets decide who imports what.
tldr.outcome: Only the hubs need the full routing table, and with ingress replication the hubs can also share the multicast copying load. The price can be an extra hop and more latency for spoke traffic.

facts.label: Hubs per spoke
facts.value: One or more; two suggested for redundancy

today: RFC 7024 is a Proposed Standard from October 2013 and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 4364 and the multicast VPN RFCs it cites.

sections.title: Hubs, Spokes and Vanilla PEs
sections.content:
With BGP/MPLS VPNs (RFC 4364), any-to-any connectivity is usually achieved by making every PE that serves a VPN hold all of that VPN's routes. This RFC lets the provider cut that down to a subset of PEs.

For a given VPN, some PEs are designated Virtual Hubs (V-hubs) and others Virtual Spokes (V-spokes). The rest are "vanilla" PEs that just follow RFC 4364. A V-hub keeps all routes of the VPN. A V-spoke keeps only the routes from its own attached sites, plus one or more VPN-IP default routes originated by its V-hubs. A VPN-IP default route is a VPN-IP route whose prefix contains only a Route Distinguisher.

Each V-spoke is associated with one or more V-hubs, and two are suggested for redundancy. A PE can be a hub for one VPN and a spoke for another. The design is a two-level hierarchy; more levels are out of scope. A V-hub and its V-spokes are assumed to be in the same Autonomous System.
sections.eli5: A few routers act as helpers who know everything. The others only know their neighbours and ask a helper for the rest.

sections.title: Routing Information Exchange
sections.content:
Sites attached to a PE are handled as in RFC 4364, whether the PE is a hub or a spoke. On top of that, a V-hub MUST export a VPN-IP default route for the VPN, and only to the V-spokes associated with it. Each V-hub MUST use a distinct Route Distinguisher for this, so a spoke that imports several default routes of equal preference shares its outbound load among the hubs.

A V-hub imports all non-default VPN-IP routes from the other PEs, but MUST NOT import a VPN-IP default route unless it is the Internet VPN-IP default route. A V-spoke MUST import the default routes from its own hubs. It MAY also import routes from other V-spokes, but only those associated with the same hubs.

These rules are built with Route Target (RT) extended communities. All hub and spoke VRFs export the VPN's usual RT-VPN, and all hubs import it. Each hub also exports its own RT-VH, which must differ from RT-VPN and cannot be shared with another VPN. A spoke becomes associated with a hub by importing that hub's RT-VH, so adding a spoke needs configuration only on the spoke. Hubs may use different RT-VHs to split the spokes among them.
sections.eli5: Routes carry coloured stickers. A helper puts its own sticker on its "ask me" note, and a spoke only picks up notes with its helper's sticker.

sections.title: Forwarding and Load Balancing
sections.content:
The label a V-hub advertises with its VPN-IP default route MUST map to an NHLFE that identifies the hub's VRF. When the hub gets a packet with that label, it pops the label and looks the destination up in the VRF. A hub MUST NOT install a default route in its VRF just because it originated the VPN-IP default route, unless that came from a default route from a CE, from the Internet VPN-IP default route, or from a VRF default route pointing at the Internet routing table.

The RFC also describes an optional procedure for a multihomed site attached to both a hub and a spoke. The hub may send packets arriving on its default-route label either to the local CE or on to the other PE, giving IBGP/EBGP load balancing. This cannot help traffic from other sites on the same spoke, because of the IP longest match rule.

Two fixes are offered. One is not to make PEs with multihomed sites into V-spokes. The other is for the spoke to re-advertise CE routes with a label whose NHLFE points at the CE instead of installing them. Traffic between sites on that spoke then goes through the hub. Implementations that support this load balancing SHOULD support the second option.
sections.eli5: If a house has two doors, the helper can send visitors through either one. A spoke that already knows the nearer door will always use it.

sections.title: Internet Connectivity
sections.content:
Two alternatives are given. In the first, a PE that holds Internet routes and a VRF of the VPN has a default route in the VRF pointing at the Internet table. It MUST NOT be a V-spoke, and if it is a V-hub it MUST originate a VPN-IP default route carrying both RT-VPN and RT-VH. Implementations MUST support this alternative.

In the second, a CE advertises an IP default route to its PE. Implementations MUST support this when the PE is a hub, and MAY support it when the PE is a spoke. A spoke in this case must not install the CE's default route. It originates a VPN-IP default route with a non-null label and only RT-VPN, so only hubs import it.

Any default route that results from these cases is called the Internet VPN-IP default route. It differs from a non-Internet one only in carrying RT-VPN as well as RT-VH. A hub originates one kind or the other at any time, never both. If the Internet route and another hub's default route have equal preference, spokes share Internet traffic across both hubs, adding an extra hub hop. To avoid that, the RFC recommends giving the Internet route higher preference.
sections.eli5: The door to the outside world gets a special sticker so every helper knows where it is. Visitors can be sent straight there instead of wandering through two helpers.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
Hubs and their spokes should be chosen to minimise the extra distance and latency, given the VPN's geographic footprint. Spokes can be grouped into geographic clusters with any-to-any connectivity inside each cluster. The RFC gives the example of a retail chain with hub-and-spoke data traffic between stores and datacenters but direct Voice over IP between nearby stores.

RT constrain (RFC 4684) may help optimise route exchange. For the customer, adding a spoke may show an extra traceroute hop (the V-hub PE) and may increase latency, depending on where the hub sits.
sections.eli5: Pick the helper who is closest to you, or asking for directions will take longer than walking.

sections.title: Multicast Support
sections.content:
Multicast VPN (MVPN) procedures from RFC 6513, RFC 6514 and RFC 6625 are adapted. The hub/spoke layout affects multicast when a source on a hub reaches a receiver on a spoke of a different hub, or when two spokes share no hub.

A V-spoke originates I-PMSI, S-PMSI and SA A-D routes as in RFC 6514, so they reach the hubs. A V-hub also adds its RT-VH to its A-D routes, and it MUST originate a second route, the Associated-V-spoke-only I-PMSI A-D route, carrying only RT-VH, with a distinct RD. Hubs do not send site traffic on that second tunnel.

When a hub receives an A-D route that carries its own RT-VH (Case 1), it must not forward the traffic to other hubs or spokes. Otherwise (Case 2), it accepts the data and forwards it onto its Associated-V-spoke-only tunnel, and it SHOULD NOT do so if no associated spoke has receivers. For S-PMSI and SA routes it MUST re-originate them toward its spokes with RT-VH. With Ingress Replication, a spoke only copies traffic to hubs, and hubs copy to their own spokes, spreading the replication load.

For I-PMSI routes using Ingress Replication, the PMSI Tunnel attribute MUST use the Ingress Replication tunnel type, set the Leaf Information Required flag to 1 and carry no MPLS labels. The receiver MUST answer with a Leaf A-D route that carries a downstream-assigned label, so it can tell the VRF and the sending PE.
sections.eli5: When one person has news for everyone, the helpers pass it along only to their own group, so nobody has to shout to the whole school.

sections.title: Example: RT Provisioning
sections.content:
VPN A has 9 sites, each on its own PE (PE-1 to PE-9). PE-3, PE-6 and PE-9 are V-hubs. PE-1 and PE-2 are spokes of PE-3, PE-4 and PE-5 are spokes of PE-6, and PE-7 and PE-8 are spokes of PE-9. Everyone exports with RT-A, and the hubs import RT-A.

Each hub originates a default route with its own RT (RT-A-VH-1, RT-A-VH-2 or RT-A-VH-3) but not RT-A, and its spokes import that RT. If site-3 has Internet access, PE-3's default route carries both RT-A and RT-A-VH-1, so PE-6, PE-9, PE-1 and PE-2 import it. If PE-7 and PE-8 want each other's routes, they export with both RT-A and RT-A-VH-3. The RFC notes that in practice each spoke should have two or more hubs.
sections.eli5: Three helpers each look after two kids. Each helper has a coloured sticker, and each pair of kids only listens for their helper's colour.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that it introduces no new security considerations above and beyond those already specified in RFC 4364. Section 9 adds an optional refinement for customers who want CEs to receive all VPN routes: the spoke keeps all VPN-IP routes in its control plane but installs only the hub's default route in its data plane. That reduces forwarding state but not control-plane resource use.
sections.eli5: It adds no new locks to worry about beyond the ones the VPN already had.
